newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK factory-gate inflation subdued in Dec.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK factory-gate inflation subdued in Dec.

text.p: British factory-gate and raw materials prices were subdued in December, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Monday, suggesting pipeline inflation pressures remain weak.
Economists said the figures would ease pressure on finance minister Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates this week to alleviate the Bank of England's worries about a resurgence in inflation.
The ONS said output prices, which reflect the cost of goods leaving factory gates, were up 0.5 percent in December from the previous month, giving a year-on-year increase of 1.7 percent.
However, the seasonally adjusted underlying rate was a modest 0.1 percent, giving an annual increase of 0.8 percent.
The ONS said the annual increase in core output prices was the lowest rate of growth in 30 years.
Input prices, a measure of the costs of raw materials and fuel, fell a seasonally adjusted 0.5 percent in December and were down 5.9 percent from a year earlier.
"Overall, these data provide further confirmation that pipeline inflation pressures remain extremely weak," said Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets.
"Coupled with last week's softer than expected data on manufacturing output and Christmas retail sales, the figures ease the pressure for a rise in interest rates after Wednesday's monetary meeting."
Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, meets central bank governor Eddie George on Wednesday for their monthly meeting on monetary policy.
The Bank has been pressing for a rise in official interest rates from 6.0 percent because it believes inflationary pressures are mounting.
But the Conservative government, which faces a general election by May at the latest, would prefer to avoid raising rates as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons.
A Reuters poll of 20 City economists last week showed 12 expected Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy, to leave rates unchanged after Wednesday's meeting.
Most of the others expect rates to rise to 6.25 percent.
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, said the fall in input prices was impressive considering the strength of oil prices.

But he noted that while input and output prices had been subdued for over a year now, this had not prevented underlying annual retail price inflation surging to 3.3 percent in October and November, well above the government's 2.5 percent target.
"It's still extremely unlikely that we'll see the government's target being met by the end of this parliament," Shaw said.
Recent comments from Clarke have suggested he wants to wait to see economic growth figures for the fourth quarter of 1996 before deciding whether to raise interest rates again.

At the October meeting when he first raised base rates, he attached great importance to third quarter gross domestic product figures. The first estimate of Q4 GDP will not be available until January 27.
